subproblem.title: Compact exhaustion K_p ⊆ interior K_{p+1} of an open set U ⊆ ℝ^N
subproblem.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ and let U ⊆ ℝ^N (= Euclidean N) be open. Then there are sets K_p ⊆ ℝ^N, p ∈ ℕ, such that every K_p is compact, K_p ⊆ U, K_p ⊆ interior K_{p+1}, the sequence is increasing (K_p ⊆ K_q whenever p ≤ q), and ⋃_p K_p = U.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (U : Set (Euclidean N)), IsOpen U → ∃ K : ℕ → Set (Euclidean N), (∀ p, IsCompact (K p)) ∧ (∀ p, K p ⊆ U) ∧ (∀ p, K p ⊆ interior (K (p + 1))) ∧ Monotone K ∧ ⋃ p, K p = U
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: the preamble of the parent proof, i.e. the compact exhaustion K_p of U used with W := interior K_{p+1}. It is re-indexed to start at p = 0, with radius p + 1 and margin 1/(p + 1).

Notation: |x| is the Euclidean norm. For a nonempty F ⊆ ℝ^N, d(x, F) := infDist x F = inf_{y ∈ F} |x − y|.

Facts used:
- x ↦ d(x, F) is continuous (Mathlib continuous_infDist_pt).
- d(x, F) = 0 for x ∈ F (infDist_zero_of_mem).
- If F is closed and nonempty, then x ∉ F iff d(x, F) > 0 (IsClosed.notMem_iff_infDist_pos).
- Closed balls of ℝ^N are compact (proper space, isCompact_closedBall), and a closed subset of a compact set is compact (IsCompact.of_isClosed_subset).
- For r > 0, interior (closedBall 0 r) = ball 0 r (interior_closedBall).

1. Case U = ℝ^N. Put K_p := closedBall(0, p + 1). Each K_p is compact and K_p ⊆ U. If |x| ≤ p + 1 then |x| < p + 2, so K_p ⊆ ball(0, p + 2) = interior closedBall(0, p + 2) = interior K_{p+1}. For p ≤ q the radii satisfy p + 1 ≤ q + 1, so K_p ⊆ K_q. Every x ∈ ℝ^N lies in K_q for any q ∈ ℕ with q ≥ |x| (Archimedean property), so ⋃_p K_p = ℝ^N = U.

2. Case U ≠ ℝ^N. Then F := ℝ^N ∖ U is nonempty, and it is closed because U is open. Put K_p := {x : |x| ≤ p + 1 and d(x, F) ≥ 1/(p + 1)}.
 (a) K_p is closed: it is the intersection of the preimages of the closed sets (−∞, p + 1] and [1/(p + 1), ∞) under the continuous maps x ↦ |x| and x ↦ d(x, F). Since K_p ⊆ closedBall(0, p + 1), which is compact, K_p is compact.
 (b) K_p ⊆ U: if x ∉ U then x ∈ F, so d(x, F) = 0 < 1/(p + 1) and x ∉ K_p.
 (c) K_p ⊆ interior K_{p+1}: the set O_p := {x : |x| < p + 2 and d(x, F) > 1/(p + 2)} is open, as a preimage of open sets under continuous maps. Also O_p ⊆ K_{p+1}, since strict inequalities imply the non-strict ones. Hence O_p ⊆ interior K_{p+1} (interior_maximal). If x ∈ K_p, then |x| ≤ p + 1 < p + 2 and d(x, F) ≥ 1/(p + 1) > 1/(p + 2), so x ∈ O_p.
 (d) Monotonicity: by (c), K_p ⊆ interior K_{p+1} ⊆ K_{p+1} for every p. By induction on q, K_p ⊆ K_q whenever p ≤ q (monotone_nat_of_le_succ).
 (e) ⋃_p K_p = U. The inclusion ⊆ is (b). Conversely, let x ∈ U. Then x ∉ F, and F is closed and nonempty, so δ := d(x, F) > 0. Choose p ∈ ℕ with 1/(p + 1) < δ (exists_nat_one_div_lt) and q ∈ ℕ with |x| ≤ q (exists_nat_ge), and put m := max(p, q). Then |x| ≤ q ≤ m ≤ m + 1 and 1/(m + 1) ≤ 1/(p + 1) < δ = d(x, F), so x ∈ K_m.

3. In both cases every K_p is compact and contained in U, K_p ⊆ interior K_{p+1}, the sequence is increasing, and its union is U. ∎
proof_key_steps: If U = ℝ^N, take K_p = closedBall(0, p+1); then K_p ⊆ ball(0, p+2) = interior K_{p+1}.
Otherwise F = ℝ^N ∖ U is closed and nonempty; K_p = {|x| ≤ p+1, d(x, F) ≥ 1/(p+1)} is closed and bounded, hence compact, and misses F.
The open set {|x| < p+2, d(x, F) > 1/(p+2)} lies between K_p and K_{p+1}, so K_p ⊆ interior K_{p+1}; monotonicity follows by induction.
Each x ∈ U has d(x, F) > 0, so x ∈ K_m for all large m; hence ⋃_p K_p = U.
